articles.title: Very severe cyclone Arnab crosses Andhra coast, weakens into severe cyclonic storm: IMD | LIVE
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The landfall process is complete with the weather system moving entirely over land; CM Naidu says no loss of life reported in Andhra

Deputy Chief Minister and Jana Sena Party president K. Pawan Kalyan has asked party workers to take part in the government’s relief and rescue work. Heavy rain is likely to continue in the coastal districts even after the cyclone crosses the coast, he said. The government is focusing on moving people from low-lying areas to relief camps and supplying food, milk and other essentials.
Andhra Pradesh has turned 609 school campuses into relief shelters for people moved from cyclone-hit areas on Wednesday. Unsafe buildings have been barricaded.
Schools in 16 coastal districts are closed, and 17,054 NCC, NSS and Scouts volunteers have been mobilised to help.
Andhra Pradesh has turned 609 schools into Cyclone Arnab relief shelters, flagged 78 buildings at risk of collapse and closed schools in 16 coastal districts.

Cyclone Arnab has weakened from a very severe to a severe cyclonic storm after completing its landfall, the IMD said on Wednesday. It crossed the coast between 2 a.m. and 8 a.m., about 20 km east-northeast of Narsapur, 40 km southwest of Yanam and 60 km southwest of Kakinada. Winds at landfall were 125 to 135 kmph, gusting to 150 kmph.- Sravani Nellore
The Kakinada police rescued four persons stranded in a Central Warehousing Corporation godown in Kakinada Anchorage Port today.

In an official release, Kakinada SP G. Bindhu Madhav has stated: “ Four staff, identified as Chintala Durga Prasad, Bommidi Anand Kumar, Soorreddi Nagaraju and Ganga Appala Raju, have been stranded in the CWC godown after water entered the godown campus”.
They spent the entire night inside the godown until the police rescued them. All of them are safe and reunited with their families. They are natives of Yanam and Kakinada.

The residents along the Kakinada coast breathed a sigh of relief this morning as winds weakened, making way for the disaster response personnel to restore the roads blocked by collapsed trees between Kakinada and Amalapuram in the Godavari region.
Scores of trees have been removed on the same route. However, no human loss has been reported anywhere in the region so far.

articles.title: No consistent improvement in Delhi’s winter air quality over four years: CREA
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: There has been no consistent improvement in Delhi’s winter air quality over the past four years, despite the imposition of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), according to an analysis of government data by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finland-based non-profit research organisation.

“Delhi’s winter AQI (Air Quality Index) has fluctuated over the past four years, with no consistent improvement. The mean AQI rose from 280 in winter 2022–23 to 304 in 2023–24, fell to 285 in 2024–25 and increased again to 295 in 2025–26. The median AQI followed a similar pattern, rising from 294 to 324, falling to 289 and then increasing to 305,” CREA said in a statement.

Delhi’s winter air quality has not followed a consistent downward trend since the 2022 revision of GRAP, and the mean and median AQI for the latest winter were both higher than in 2022–23, said Manoj Kumar, an analyst at CREA.

The mean and median of the AQI are statistical measures used to summarize air quality data over a specific period. Because AQI levels can fluctuate wildly due to weather changes or pollution spikes, these two metrics tell different stories about the air you breathe.

GRAP comprises short-term emergency measures to reduce air pollution and is divided into four stages, depending on the level of pollution recorded or forecast for the near future. The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (CAQM) announces the different stages based on air quality forecasts.

Every winter, air pollution levels rise in Delhi-NCR and several parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP), mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and falling temperatures. Stubble burning during October and November, along with firecracker emissions, further worsens pollution.
Meanwhile, Delhi’s air quality remained in the ‘poor’ category for the second consecutive day on Thursday.

The 24-hour average AQI stood at 223 (poor) at 4 p.m. on Thursday, down from 245 (poor) a day earlier, according to the Central Pollution Control Board’s (CPCB) daily bulletin, which provides the official AQI for the day.

The CAQM held separate review meetings with the governments of Punjab and Haryana in Chandigarh on Thursday to assess measures to prevent and control paddy stubble burning and reduce other major sources of air pollution. It directed the States to take prompt action on the ground.

The Commission emphasised the need to strengthen the crop-residue supply chain and ensure the effective utilisation of available machinery during the peak harvesting period. The meetings also covered field verification of burnt-area assessments based on satellite fire alerts, along with the district-wise deployment of drones and low-cost sensors to monitor stubble-burning incidents.

articles.title: Federal Reserve likely to skip rate hike despite elevated inflation
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, wants to return inflation to its 2% target, which it typically does by raising its short-term interest rate. Higher borrowing costs, over time, can cool spending and slow inflation

The Federal Reserve is expected to stand pat on interest rates on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) even though inflation has accelerated in the past couple of months as the Iran war has caused spikes in oil and gas prices.

The Fed's latest policy meeting concludes less than a week before the midterm elections, which have focused heavily on concerns about the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items.

The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, wants to return inflation to its 2% target, which it typically does by raising its short-term interest rate. Higher borrowing costs, over time, can cool spending and slow inflation. The Fed raised its key rate last month for the first time in three years, from about 3.6% to 3.9%, in what many investors and economists perceived was a first step toward a renewed effort to bring down inflation.

Yet Mr. Warsh faces a host of challenges in achieving that goal. President Donald Trump slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Mr. Warsh, whom he appointed. And some of the forces driving inflation — specifically the rapid build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won't easily be tamed by higher interest rates.

At the same time, other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans' sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.

After the Fed announces its rate decision, Mr. Warsh will speak at a news conference, where his remarks will be closely watched for hints about the Fed's next steps. He will likely repeat the Fed's desire for a “timelier” return of inflation to the 2% target. Some may view that as a sign the Fed will boost its key rate at its next meeting, in December, a move already widely expected by Wall Street investors.

If the Fed keeps rates on hold, Mr. Warsh will be pushed to explain why the central bank hiked rates in September but not this month. Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.

And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely-followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed's 2% target.

On Thursday (October 29, 2026), a separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.

Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics at Bank of America, said economists and the Fed have gotten too complacent about above-target inflation. Higher oil and gas prices will likely keep inflation elevated for several more months, he said, and rising diesel costs will elevate shipping prices for nearly every type of good, which could spread inflation more broadly through the economy.

articles.title: First Israeli election exit polls show narrow edge for Opposition
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Israel’s current Opposition chief Yair Lapid said Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc had suffered a “crushing defeat”, while left-wing leader Yair Golan said the public had “fired the Netanyahu government”

The first exit polls from Israel’s elections showed the opposition bloc with a slight edge over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp as voting ended Tuesday (October 27, 2026), but still shy of an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

The country’s main pollsters -- Channels 11, 12 and 13 -- projected the Opposition bloc to win 52 or 53 seats, and Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc to win 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in the parliament, with 24 or 25 seats.

Israeli Arab parties also made gains after their voter base turned out in high numbers. The exit polls showed the two Arab-majority groupings, Raam and the Joint List, winning 17 or 18 seats between them.

In the last election, Likud walked away with 32 seats, enabling it to cobble together a coalition with smaller far-right parties after Mr. Netanyahu’s traditional allies baulked at the corruption cases the premier was facing.

This time around, those mainstream right-wing parties, by and large, vowed to work with main challenger Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party -- projected to nab 21 to 23 seats -- to form an Opposition coalition capable of unseating Netanyahu.
“The initial exit poll results indicate a complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the October 7 government,” Mr. Eisenkot said.
Israel’s current Opposition chief Yair Lapid said Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc had suffered a “crushing defeat”, while left-wing leader Yair Golan said the public had “fired the Netanyahu government”.
While Raam and the Joint List do not belong to the Opposition bloc, they have expressed openness to supporting it.
Tuesday’s (October 27, 2026) poll was marked by high turnout, with many voters saying they saw it as pivotal for the country’s future.
The following is a party-by-party breakdown of the projected seat count in the first exit polls

articles.title: Trump drastically loosens oil and gas methane rules
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Mr. Trump is pushing ways of bringing down energy costs ahead of the midterms, amid voter anger over soaring oil costs caused by his war on Iran
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas super pollutant.
Mr. Trump made the announcement at a rally in support of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who faces a tough battle for a U.S. Senate seat in November 3 midterm elections.
The regulations were put in place by Republican Trump's Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.
"Tonight, I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion," Mr. Trump said at the rally in Lubbock, Texas.
To cheers from the crowd, Mr. Trump added that the move would "unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas." Texas is by far the country's leading fossil-fuel-producing state.
An Environmental Protection Agency statement earlier this month gave the same $45 billion figure in cost savings, without offering a detailed breakdown of the savings.

"Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work," said EPA administrator Lee Zeldin. "They can't do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens."
Mr. Trump is pushing ways of bringing down energy costs ahead of the midterms, amid voter anger over soaring oil costs caused by his war on Iran.
Polls show Republicans could lose control of Congress to the Democrats in next week's vote.

Methane, the main component of natural gas, is the second-largest cause of global warming behind carbon dioxide — responsible for about a third, or 0.5°C, of total planetary heating since the pre-industrial era.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas super pollutant.

Mr. Trump is pushing ways of bringing down energy costs ahead of the midterms, amid voter anger over soaring oil costs caused by his war on Iran.

articles.title: Two Britons charged in connection with assisting Iran over U.K. airbase incident
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: British-Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir, both aged 24 and from London, were charged under the National Security Act, U.K. prosecutors say
Two British nationals have been charged under the U.K.’s National Security Act in connection with an incident at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford airbase on September 27, 2026.
Nouman Essghir, 24, and Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, from London, were charged and scheduled to appear in court this week.

Mr. Abdulkarim was arrested for allegedly assisting a foreign intelligence service. The country was believed to be Iran , according to Laurence Taylor, the Head of the U.K.’s National Counterterrorism Policing unit.
Five men were arrested as they approached the air base in three vans on September 27. This resulted in the evacuation of residents in the air base area in Gloucestershire.
Essghir was initially released on bail before being re-arrested last week. Abdulkarim was arrested in the past week. Six other men have been arrested and released on bail as investigations continue.

British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
The suspects were subsequently released on police bail, which led to criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump.
An Iranian-British dual national was later arrested (and released on police bail) in early October.
Following the incident, the U.S. had removed its 12 B-1 Bombers , used in its strikes on Iran, from the airbase.

articles.title: U.S., Cuba shouting match derails debate at UN
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The row broke out during debate on a resolution calling for an end to the U.S. embargo on its communist-led neighbour, a non-binding measure which Cuba has put forward every year since 1992
A furious shouting match between representatives of the United States and Cuba prompted the temporary suspension of debate at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).
The row broke out during debate on a resolution calling for an end to the U.S. embargo on its communist-led neighbour, a non-binding measure which Cuba has put forward every year since 1992.
The debate this year, however, is taking place amid a major new pressure campaign by Washington against Cuba, including an oil blockade and broad sanctions that have severely crippled Cuba's economy.
As U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz was addressing the General Assembly, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez objected to the remarks and walked up to the podium, demanding that the speech be halted.
Mr. Waltz, while arguing for the resolution to be rejected, had been criticising repression of Cuban citizens by the communist government.
"This is the United Nations. This isn't your communist dictatorship. You cannot silence me," Mr. Waltz shouted, demanding that Mr. Rodriguez and other Cuban diplomats back away.
The chair briefly suspended the session and instructed both countries’ representatives to return to their places, after which Mr. Waltz was allowed to continue.
Cuba has accused Washington of launching an "unprecedented" pressure campaign this year to persuade countries to oppose the resolution, which has traditionally had overwhelming backing.
ALSO WATCH Cuba power crisis worsens after another grid collapse
Last year, the resolution received 165 votes in favor, seven against and 12 abstentions, its weakest level of support in two decades.

articles.title: What is ‘human composting’ — how does it work?
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: What should happen to your body after you die? It’s hardly a topic you’d bring up over dinner, but it’s a decision that will eventually need to be made, either by you or by those you leave behind.

In Australia, the choice has traditionally been between burial and cremation. However, concerns about environmental impact, limited cemetery space and the desire for more sustainable alternatives have encouraged interest in other approaches.
These include natural burial, water cremation and shrouded cremation — where no coffin is used.

Now, New South Wales has become the first Australian state to pass legislation allowing another option: “human composting”, technically known as natural organic reduction, and legally termed “terramation”. The process uses microorganisms to transform human remains into a compost-like material.
📢 So-called terramation will become legal in NSW, with several MPs revealing they want their own bodies turned into soil after they die. [image or embed]
The idea of turning a human body into compost might sound unusual, or even unsettling. But how does it actually work? Is it a better alternative to existing methods?
To answer these questions, we first need to understand decomposition and its essential role in nature.
Throughout history, humans have developed rituals to protect, preserve and dress the dead. Some want a quick return to the earth, while others seek to preserve the body.
From ancient burial vessels and elaborate tombs to coffins, shrouds and embalming, these practices reflect cultural and religious beliefs. They also affect how bodies decompose.
Decomposition begins shortly after death. As cells break down, microorganisms already living inside the body, along with those from the surrounding environment, begin breaking down its tissues.

articles.title: Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Finding ways to track Starlink ‌users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals

Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink’s ‌satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.

Researchers at ​TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro, concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ⁠ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.

The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI’s telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink ‌users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted. Bidding refers to the complex auction system by which advertisers secure space inside people’s browsers and apps.
SpaceX ‌did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two ‌weeks.

TrendAI ⁠released a report on October 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party ⁠responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79.” The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.

TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding “hype-driven labels” or “unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort ​risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions.”

Finding ways to track Starlink ‌users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals. Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields. Starlink has become a particularly important resource in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service for frontline communications and directing drone ‌strikes.

In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and ​track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process.
The same day that TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology ⁠firm Confiant outed Discover-Tech by name.
Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder.

articles.title: India among top countries with highest heatwave exposure for infants, older adults: Report
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Globally, total number of heatwave days decreased from 2024’s historical high of 15.3 billion person-days for older adults and 2.3 billion person-days for infants

India ranked among the top countries with the highest heatwave exposure for both vulnerable age groups — infants and older adults — along with China, the U.S. and Russia, according to the tenth indicator report of the Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change.

Globally, total number of heatwave days decreased from 2024's historical high of 15.3 billion person-days for older adults and 2.3 billion person-days for infants. The year 2025 was the second highest on record for heatwave exposure for both vulnerable groups combined as older adults were exposed to 10.8 billion person-days of heatwaves, while infants experienced 1.1 billion person-days, the report said.
When normalised by population size, older adults experienced on average 12.8 heatwave days per individual in 2025, while infants experienced on average 8.7 heatwave days per individual, it said.

Authors of the report, led by those at the U.K.'s University College London, said climate action is picking up around the world, but failing to keep pace with global warming, especially as health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the 2016 Paris Agreement, compared to the previous one.

A decade after the Paris Agreement, the report's authors are calling for climate change to be formally declared a global health emergency, for a new WHO instrument to enable a coordinated global response, and for governments to put health at the centre of every climate decision, from emissions targets to climate funding.

Priorities include urgent, fair cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, sustained investment in science, and climate finance for health delivered as grants rather than loans, so that countries can adapt without taking on more debt, they said.

"A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world's response to them, and in many cases even accelerating," author Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, professor at University College London, said.
Real progress has been made in clean energy, health system readiness, and health-protective regulation, all of which are already delivering health benefits to local communities, Ms. Romanello said.

"However, progress has been too slow, too small, and isn't reaching those who need it most. That is why we are calling for climate change to be formally recognised as a global health emergency, with health placed at the centre of every climate decision," Ms. Romanello said.

articles.title: Growing economic inequality one of nation's most pressing concerns, government must act: Congress
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Opposition party also said that claims of economic development are meaningful only when their benefits reach the common man

Asserting that "growing economic inequality" is one of India's "most pressing concerns", the Congress on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) demanded that the government acknowledge the reality of this "economic distress", expand employment opportunities, and take concrete steps to rein in inflation.

The Opposition party also said that claims of economic development are meaningful only when their benefits reach the common man; otherwise, these statistics tell a story not of progress, but of a widening economic divide.

Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh shared on X a media report that claimed that households invested more money in bank deposits, mutual funds, and other financial assets, but their 'new debt' grew much faster; as a result, net household financial savings declined by about 4% to 21.6₹9 lakh crore in the 2025-26 fiscal year, compared to ₹22.57 lakh crore last year.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge also attacked the Modi government, alleging that it is desperate to strip away voting rights and now also wants to eliminate the right to live as well.

"Amidst festivals, back-breaking inflation, is gobbling up every single penny of earnings. The numbers tell the truth - Food inflation: Rose from 2.13% to 7.74; Household debt: Up 36.7%, at triple the pace; Household financial savings: Down 4%; Retail inflation: 5.54%; Wholesale inflation: 11.39%," Kharge said in his post in Hindi on X.

"If the BJP, now sitting in power and staging sit-ins today, and Mr. Modi ever find time away from their senseless grandstanding, they should rewatch their own 'Bahut hui mehengaai' ad from before 2014. The public has wasted 12 years waiting for the promise of 'achche din'," he said.

In his post in Hindi, Mr. Ramesh said, "Badhti mehengaai, barhta karz, ghat-ti kamaai, Modi sarkar mein madhyam warg ke hisse aayi sirf tabahi (Rising inflation, mounting debt, shrinking earnings - Under the Modi government, the middle class has faced nothing but devastation)."
Mr. Ramesh alleged that the Modi government is manipulating data to conceal the true extent of inflation.

"The younger generation is bearing the brunt of a declining economy and dwindling employment opportunities. Data indicates that companies are hiring less, and people are even losing long-held jobs," he said.
Incomes and savings are steadily declining in the face of rising inflation, he argued.

articles.title: Lecturers deputed for Hasanamba festival duty in Hassan
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Hassan district administration has deputed 13 pre-university college lecturers from government colleges to handle public announcement systems on the Hasanamba temple premises during the Hasanamba festival, which begins on Thursday.

Hassan Deputy Commissioner K.S. Latha Kumari, in an order, formed the Hasanamba Utsava Information Announcers Management Team-2026 with 14 members, of whom 13 are lecturers. The lecturers have been directed to make public announcements instructing devotees waiting in queues on queue management, darshan timings and other arrangements.

The decision has not gone down well with the lecturers’ community. A group of lecturers, led by District Lecturers’ Association president Sanne Gowda, met Excise Minister K.M. Shivalinge Gowda, who is also the district in-charge Minister, and the Assistant Commissioner, who is the administrator of the temple, on Tuesday. They appealed for the order to be withdrawn, saying that engaging lecturers for such a long period would affect teaching.

“The Department of PU Education has instructed us to complete the syllabus before December and begin preparatory examinations. If lecturers are engaged in festival duty, teaching will suffer,” Mr. Sanne Gowda said.

The PU Department has often issued instructions restricting lecturers from taking up any work other than teaching. “We are not even allowed to attend the academic enhancement programmes organised by our lecturers’ forums, which are forced to conduct such activities on holidays. Yet the district administration has involved lecturers in festival duty,” pointed out a lecturer who did not wish to be named.

articles.title: Cyclone Arnab claims five lives in Andhra Pradesh; Naidu announces relief package
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: ₹5 lakh ex gratia for each victim; aid announced for farmers, fishermen, households and businesses

Cyclone Arnab claimed five lives in Andhra Pradesh, prompting Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu to announce a comprehensive relief and compensation package for affected families, farmers, fishermen and businesses.
Expressing condolences to the bereaved families, he said the government had made extensive efforts to minimise casualties and property damage.

Addressing a press conference at the Secretariat on Wednesday, the Chief Minister identified the deceased as Amrapinni Devmud and Kolamuru Madhavi from the Visakhapatnam region, Chukkala Kishore from Bhimavaram, Bhagyalakshmi from Anakapalli and Kollu Venkayamma from Sakretipalli.

Mr. Devmud died after a tree fell on an electric wire, while Ms. Madhavi died after an electric pole fell on her. Mr. Kishore was killed when a palm tree fell on him, and Ms. Bhagyalakshmi died of electrocution. Ms. Venkayamma died when a wall collapsed on her while she was travelling in a passenger vehicle. The families of each deceased person would receive an ex gratia payment of ₹5 lakh, Mr. Naidu said.
He urged people to remain cautious even after the cyclone crossed the coast.

Families whose houses were inundated would receive 25 kg of rice, while fishermen’s families and handloom households would get 50 kg. Each affected family would also receive one kg each of red gram, onions, sugar and potatoes, besides one litre of palm oil. Those staying in relief camps would receive ₹1,000 per person, subject to a ceiling of ₹3,000 per family.

Partially damaged houses would receive ₹10,000 in compensation. Damaged grocery shops, restaurants and service establishments would be given ₹25,000. Micro, small and medium enterprises with an annual turnover below ₹40 lakh would receive ₹50,000, those with a turnover between ₹40 lakh and ₹1.5 crore ₹1 lakh, and those exceeding ₹1.5 crore ₹1.5 lakh.

Compensation of ₹3,000 would be paid for damaged two-wheelers and ₹10,000 for motorised three-wheelers. Pushcart owners would receive ₹20,000, while weavers and specified artisans would get ₹25,000. Those who lost raw materials would be given ₹10,000.

Fishermen would receive ₹9,000 for partially damaged boats and nets, ₹5,000 for net repairs and ₹10,000 for replacement nets. Compensation would be ₹20,000 for fully damaged non-motorised boats with nets and ₹25,000 for fully damaged fishing boats with nets. Fish farms would receive ₹18,000, while damaged sericulture sheds would be eligible for ₹25,000.

Livestock compensation would include ₹50,000 for a cow, ₹40,000 for a buffalo, ₹25,000 for specified livestock categories and ₹7,500 for each sheep or goat. Assistance of ₹100 per poultry bird would be provided, subject to a ceiling of ₹10,000. Owners of damaged cattle sheds would receive ₹5,000.

articles.title: 93-year-old woman donates ₹1 lakh from pension towards children’s education
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Makam Dhanamma contributed from her pooled funds after being approached for help by litterateurs and language enthusiasts affiliated with the Bala Vikas Vedika, Sarvajna Publications and Nemileti Publishers
Despite her old age and lack of formal education, a 93-year-old woman donated ₹1 lakh from her family pension to the cause of children’s education as an act of service to the society.

Makam Dhanamma (93) is the widow of late Makam Subramanyam Chetty, who hailed from Mogili Venkatagiri in Chittoor district. Subramanyam Chetty retired as a higher grade school teacher in 1978 and received a monthly pension in a two-digit figure. After his demise, her family pension has increased to ₹20,000.

Recently, litterateurs and language enthusiasts Harish, B.V. Ramana and Nemileti Kittanna, representing the Bala Vikas Vedika, Sarvajna Publications and Nemileti Publishers respectively, called on her and sought her help for the cause of children’s education. She responded to their request by donating ₹1 lakh from her pooled up money.

“Dhanamma immediately handed over ₹1 lakh towards the publication of children’s such like Ma Thatha Cheppina Kathalu , Padya Parijathalu and for the purchase of a telescope to aid sky gazing activities among school students,” recalls Sakam Nagaraja, the president of Progressive Writers Association (Abhyudaya Rachayithala Sangam – ARASAM).

Meanwhile, Dhanamma expressed concern over children dropping out from schools due to lack of financial resources. With her excellent memory, she even recalled interesting anecdotes from her childhood days.

“Being the LoP @RahulGandhi, I suggest you refrain from politicising every issue. “Tata is being criminally destroyed and no business leader dares say a word. How long will you stay silent? Until they own you? Indian business is not Modi and Shah’s plaything,” Mr. Gandhi said, adding, “You lack courage. We don’t. We will ensure justice for these crimes.”

articles.title: BIS seizes Ninja brand kitchen appliances worth ₹8 crore
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) seized 13,021 Ninja brand kitchen appliances worth approximately ₹8 crore for allegedly violating mandatory quality certification requirements during a search operation at a company’s premises in Bengaluru on Tuesday.

The BIS Bengaluru Branch Office conducted the operation at Cavitak Global Commerce Pvt. Ltd., which operates under the brand name GRIPIT, at Chagalahatti, near CMR College Road in Jala Hobli, Yelahanka.
The seized goods comprised 8,713 air fryers and 4,308 portable blenders that did not bear the mandatory BIS Standard Mark (ISI mark).
Four air fryers and one portable blender were also taken to the BIS office as evidence, according to the seizure memo.

The action was taken under Section 28 of the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016, for alleged violations of mandatory certification requirements. The appliances were found to be non-compliant with the Electrical Appliances for Kitchen (Quality Control) Order, 2023.

The BIS said that legal proceedings would be initiated against the company based on the findings. The operation forms part of the bureau’s ongoing efforts to prevent the sale of products that fail to meet prescribed quality and safety standards, thereby protecting consumers from non-compliant goods.
The BIS advised consumers to check for the ISI mark on products covered under mandatory certification and verify licence details through the BIS Care app.
Consumers can also report suspected violations through the bureau’s official website at www.bis.gov.in.

articles.title: On the question of KIIFB’s future
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: An expert panel constituted by Keralam’s UDF government to review the functioning of KIIFB has recommended winding it up and absorbing its functions into the State government, prompting a closer look at the merits of off-budget borrowings by States and the need to boost public investment in Keralam

In July, Keralam’s newly elected UDF government set up an expert panel to review the functioning of Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board (KIIFB). The panel, headed by a former civil servant, was tasked with recommending measures to restructure KIIFB and strengthen the government’s institutional capabilities, among other things. The committee has recently submitted its report, which has been tabled in the State Assembly.

Apparently critical of KIIFB’s functioning, the committee has recommended winding it up; absorbing its functions and capabilities into the State government, news reports say. The principal reason for the panel’s recommendation is that with the clubbing of KIIFB’s borrowing function with the State budget, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) has lost its primary purpose.

KIIFB, restructured by the LDF government, reportedly boosted the State’s infrastructure investment by raising extra-budgetary resources, including securing soft loans known as “Masala Bonds” from international agencies after the disastrous floods of 2019. However, the SPV’s functioning and financial performance have remained contentious. The comptroller and auditor general’s (CAG) strictures against KIIFB have become a convenient beating stick for the Centre and the Opposition parties in the State. Leftist critics have branded it as the arm of “the Left Managerial State” for promoting controversial projects, bypassing legislative approvals. We seek to explain them, intending to shed some light on the contentious issue.

Keralam reportedly spends a mere 1.5 per cent of the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) on infrastructure. This was so in spite of Keralam’s own-tax revenue to GSDP ratio being among the highest among major States, as per the RBI data.

KIIFB was set up in 1999 and underwent a major restructuring in 2016; the institution’s record in expanding public goods is apparently well acknowledged. However, its functioning raised many queries. The CAG found that the SPV’s finances flouted its procedural audits, which became a sticking point between the Centre and the State. Moreover, as KIIFB functioned outside the purview of the State budget, without generating financial profits from its lending, its borrowings being serviced out of the State’s revenue became the heart of the contention.

In the good/bad old days of “planning”, State finances broadly followed the “gap-filling” approach; meaning the Centre made up the difference between a State’s projected revenue growth and its “developmental needs” as per the State plans. It was a negotiated process, part financial and part political. Evidence shows that richer and politically influential States got the lion’s share of the divisible pool of the plan resources.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBM) 2003 changed that by seemingly imposing a “hard budget constraint”, with the fiscal deficit capped at 3 per cent of GSDP. The RBI now monitors the size of the State debt. The coupon (interest) rate of the State loans depends on the State’s debt sustainability measures. The hard budget constraint has reportedly improved State finances, or at a minimum, made them transparent.

However, most States have devised a variety of means for securing extra-budgetary resources, or off-budget borrowings (OBBs) – as evident from the RBI’s compilation of State finances. The CAG, tracking OBBs, finds that there is a bewildering variety of them. And the actual OBBs are far higher than what it is able to count, as per its own findings. In other words, ensuring fiscal discipline seems like a cat-and-mouse game between the Centre and States. Incidentally, Keralam is not among the worst offenders.

Globally, a variety of financial institutions and fiscal arrangements have existed outside of the budgetary process. Numerous kinds of para-statal organisations are a feature – not a bug – of the fiscal landscape, especially among fast-growing Asian economies. China, for instance, has a bewildering variety of financial arrangements that enable provinces to draw resources from the national development banks to sustain employment at the local level, augment production and exports and ensure political stability. No wonder, China’s public debt to GDP ratio is nearly 300 per cent – though most of it domestic.

Then, realistically, what should be the rules for managing extra-budgetary resources and institutions for Keralam? Simply speaking, if extra-budgetary resources are productively used and they comply with the government expenditure principles, having such off-budget institutions/borrowings may not be undesirable. This follows the Domar rule: so long as the output growth rate exceeds the interest rate on such loans (either at current or at constant prices), they are being used productively. Since such investments have a public good character, individual projects may not be yielding adequate revenue or covering the full costs. However, if in the aggregate they contribute to growth in state output (GSDP) and follow the Domar rule, then such investments are in principle viable.

articles.title: What the new E100 vehicle rules mean | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing

The story so far: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 , to permit the use of ethanol-based fuels containing up to 100% ethanol (E100) in vehicles. The move paves the way for flex-fuel vehicles, which can run on petrol, ethanol blends of varying proportions, or pure ethanol.
The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing.

One of the key changes is the inclusion of E100, or fuel comprising 100% ethanol, alongside E85 in several tables under Rule 115. E85 is a fuel containing up to 85% ethanol, while E100 consists entirely of ethanol, subject to applicable fuel specifications.
The amendments include an explanatory note stating that E85 or E100 may be used only in flex-fuel vehicles designed by original equipment manufacturers.

No. In a press statement, the Ministry sought to allay concerns among motorists, clarifying that a vehicle’s compatibility with E10 or E20 does not establish its suitability for E85. The notification does not require owners of existing vehicles to switch to E85 or modify their vehicles, either now or in the future.

Motorists should check the fuel-compatibility sticker on their vehicle and follow the manufacturer’s guidance in the owner’s manual when choosing fuel at a filling station, the Ministry statement added.

The amendments are expected to facilitate homologation, the official certification process through which authorised agencies, such as the Automotive Research Association of India, verify that vehicles and components comply with technical, safety and environmental standards before they can be approved for sale or use on public roads.
This will help secure type approvals for E100-powered vehicles, supporting their rollout and wider consumer adoption.
Corrections have also been incorporated into fuel classifications, including a reference to gasoline blended with 20% ethanol, or E20, in place of an earlier notation referring to E10.

India achieved its 20% ethanol-blending (E20) target in 2025 , five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. From April 2026, all Bharat Stage-VI (BS-VI) vehicles are required to fully meet E20 emission standards, and all petrol sold across India is mandated to contain 20% ethanol (E20). The policy focus is now widening beyond E20: the government has enabled the regulatory pathway for E85 and E100 vehicles, though these fuels will require compatible flex-fuel vehicles and dedicated dispensing infrastructure.

articles.title: Two trains collide in Spain’s Toledo Province; at least 30 dead
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital, Madrid, to Seville in southwestern Spain

A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) in central Spain, according to local media.
Spanish authorities initially reported 10 deaths, but Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, added “that number will surely rise.”
Spanish state-owned news agency EFE and other media reported later that the death toll had risen to at least 30.

People check an information screen displaying a message that the high-speed train line between Madrid and Andalucia has been interrupted following the collision of two high-speed trains between the towns of Mora and Orgaz at Atocha train station in Madrid, Spain, on October 28, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters
It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning (October 28, 2026) in the Province of Toledo. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Ms. Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital, Madrid, to Seville in southwestern Spain. One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García told TVE that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.
“It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy,” Mr. García said.

articles.title: Israel elections: Understanding how Knesset polls work vs India’s system
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Israel’s political clash after the October 27 national vote pits Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu against former military chief Gadi Eisenkot in a neck-and-neck fight to form a government, as neither major bloc won a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset
Israel faces a high-stakes political standoff after the October 27 national election, the country’s first vote since the 2023 Hamas attack.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, have both claimed a mandate to form the next government after exit polls showed their respective camps in a neck-and-neck fight without an outright majority, leaving the outcome dependent on the final seat tally and negotiations with smaller parties.

The main difference between Israeli and Indian elections lies in how votes translate into seats. Israel operates under a nationwide system of proportional representation, treating the country as a single voting constituency without separate geographic districts or local MPs. Israelis do not vote for individual candidates. Instead, they cast a single ballot for a closed party list and the 120 seats in parliament, known as the Knesset, are allocated in direct proportion to each party’s share of the national vote.

Meanwhile, India employs a first-past-the-post system (FPTP) across 543 parliamentary constituencies. Indian citizens cast ballots for local candidates in their respective constituencies and whichever candidate secures a majority vote in a constituency wins that seat.

No single political party has ever won an outright 61-seat majority in Israel’s history. With the exit polls on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) too predicting no outright majority for any bloc, forming a coalition government appears to be their only way to go. To enter the 120-seat Knesset, a political list must clear an electoral threshold of 3.25% of the national vote, which equals roughly four seats. Parties that fall short of this line lose all their votes without representation, making party mergers and alliances pertinent ahead of candidate submission deadlines.

For instance, Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition comprises his own right-wing party Likud, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s pro-settler Religious ⁠Zionism and ​National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power.

To form a ruling government in Israel, a coalition must assemble at least 61 seats. This is a requirement that grants small niche factions a disproportionate sway as political kingmakers. If internal divisions cause a minor party to withdraw its support, the entire administration can quickly fall apart. In contrast, Indian political parties frequently build post-poll or pre-poll alliances. Additionally, major national parties in India can and often do win single-party majority mandates without relying on minor regional partners for survival.

In India, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party secured outright single-party majority in back-to-back general elections, winning 282 seats in 2014 and 303 seats in 2019, well above the 272-seat majority mark in the 543-member Lok Sabha. But in the 2024 general elections, the PM Modi-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) bagged only 286 seats, with the BJP winning 240 seats and falling 32 short of the majority mark of 272 seats, prompting a coalition with their allies.

After the official results are published, Israel President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of the elected parliamentary factions before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.
The President generally selects the candidate considered best placed to secure parliamentary support, rather than being required to choose the leader of the largest party.

🌐 International & Geopolitics 📅 28 Oct 2026 ⏱️ 4 Min Read

📰 Israel elections: Understanding how Knesset polls work vs India’s system

🎯 Exam Relevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

Israel’s political clash after the October 27 national vote pits Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu against former military chief Gadi Eisenkot in a neck-and-neck fight to form a government, as neither major bloc won a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset

Israel faces a high-stakes political standoff after the October 27 national election, the country’s first vote since the 2023 Hamas attack.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, have both claimed a mandate to form the next government after exit polls showed their respective camps in a neck-and-neck fight without an outright majority, leaving the outcome dependent on the final seat tally and negotiations with smaller parties.

The main difference between Israeli and Indian elections lies in how votes translate into seats. Israel operates under a nationwide system of proportional representation, treating the country as a single voting constituency without separate geographic districts or local MPs. Israelis do not vote for individual candidates. Instead, they cast a single ballot for a closed party list and the 120 seats in parliament, known as the Knesset, are allocated in direct proportion to each party’s share of the national vote.

Meanwhile, India employs a first-past-the-post system (FPTP) across 543 parliamentary constituencies. Indian citizens cast ballots for local candidates in their respective constituencies and whichever candidate secures a majority vote in a constituency wins that seat.

No single political party has ever won an outright 61-seat majority in Israel’s history. With the exit polls on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) too predicting no outright majority for any bloc, forming a coalition government appears to be their only way to go. To enter the 120-seat Knesset, a political list must clear an electoral threshold of 3.25% of the national vote, which equals roughly four seats. Parties that fall short of this line lose all their votes without representation, making party mergers and alliances pertinent ahead of candidate submission deadlines.

For instance, Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition comprises his own right-wing party Likud, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s pro-settler Religious ⁠Zionism and ​National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power.

To form a ruling government in Israel, a coalition must assemble at least 61 seats. This is a requirement that grants small niche factions a disproportionate sway as political kingmakers. If internal divisions cause a minor party to withdraw its support, the entire administration can quickly fall apart. In contrast, Indian political parties frequently build post-poll or pre-poll alliances. Additionally, major national parties in India can and often do win single-party majority mandates without relying on minor regional partners for survival.

In India, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party secured outright single-party majority in back-to-back general elections, winning 282 seats in 2014 and 303 seats in 2019, well above the 272-seat majority mark in the 543-member Lok Sabha. But in the 2024 general elections, the PM Modi-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) bagged only 286 seats, with the BJP winning 240 seats and falling 32 short of the majority mark of 272 seats, prompting a coalition with their allies.

After the official results are published, Israel President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of the elected parliamentary factions before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.

The President generally selects the candidate considered best placed to secure parliamentary support, rather than being required to choose the leader of the largest party.

1. Core Context & Background: Israel’s political clash after the October 27 national vote pits Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu against former military chief Gadi Eisenkot in a neck-and-neck fight to form a government, as neither major bloc won a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Israel faces a high-stakes political standoff after the October 27 national election, the country’s first vote since the 2023 Hamas attack.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The President generally selects the candidate considered best placed to secure parliamentary support, rather than being required to choose the leader of the largest party.

articles.title: Israel polls: Golan urges Eisenkot's bloc to form government with Arab parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Several allies in the Opposition's change bloc have rejected the proposal to include Arab parties in a governing coalition, while some have also ruled out relying on their support from outside

Yair Golan, leader of Israel's Democratic Party, on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) urged the Opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to form a government in partnership with Arab-led parties to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, highlighting divisions within the opposition over such cooperation.
Several allies in the Opposition's "change bloc" have rejected the proposal to include Arab parties in a governing coalition, while some have also ruled out relying on their support from outside.
"Netanyahu lost. I know how to count to 120. 65 is more than 55. That's how Israeli democracy works. Period," Mr. Golan, a former deputy chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF), wrote on X.
Mr. Golan called for an end to what he described as racism and fear of political cooperation with Arab citizens.

"The picture of reality must teach us one resounding lesson: We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't stop with the racism. We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he wrote.

"The voice of an Israeli citizen voting in Taybeh is worth exactly as much as the voice of an Israeli citizen voting in Givat Shmuel. No less. Not approximately. Exactly," he said, arguing that Arab citizens' votes should carry the same weight as those of Jewish citizens.
"Anyone who tries to erase the voices of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel," he added.

Mr. Golan's proposal faces resistance from Opposition figures who have ruled out forming a government that includes Arab-led parties. The Opposition remains divided over whether Arab parties should join a governing coalition or support it from outside.
Mr. Golan also challenged Mr. Netanyahu's allies over their claims to represent Zionism, criticising ultra-Orthodox parties in the Prime Minister's bloc for opposing universal military conscription.
"In Netanyahu's bloc sit 16 Knesset members from non-Zionist Haredi parties, who promote mass draft evasion while our children are fighting and dying," Mr. Golan wrote.

articles.title: Real Madrid apologise to Chinese people over Mbappe's Mao 'dictator' comment
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "We take seriously the apology ‌that the person has made"

On Tuesday (October 27, 2026), Chinese brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc ‌Beverage ceased all cooperation with Mbappe, who apologised for his comment.

In a video on ‌a French podcast that has since been ‌taken ⁠down, Mbappe is heard discussing a funny ⁠meme where his face had been photoshopped on to that of "some guy — I think he's a Chinese dictator".
"Real Madrid CF wishes ​to express its ‌apologies to the Chinese people for any discomfort caused by the recent words of our player Kylian Mbappe," Real said in a statement.

"Our club ‌maintains a deep respect for China, its history, ​its culture and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese ⁠fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid," the statement added.

The backlash highlighted the risks for ‌athletes and brands in the lucrative Chinese market, where satire about Mao, modern China's founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo.
Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe's face on images ‌of military and political leaders to suggest that he has ​the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for.
Mbappe has been nicknamed "the ⁠dictator" in the European press.
On Wednesday (October 28, 2026), when asked what ⁠China thought of Mbappe's apology, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "We take seriously the apology ‌that the person has made."

articles.title: Indian Patent Office rejects patent application for drug-resistant TB regimen
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Civil society groups urge U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development to withdraw related patent claims in other countries

The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), a six-month, all-oral treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Third World Network (TWN) welcomed the development.
Recommended by the WHO for eligible people, BPaL offers a shorter course of treatment than older, longer regimens, reducing the burden of treatment on patients and their families.

“Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections. Access to a shorter, oral and effective treatment can mean returning to work, caring for their families and rebuilding their lives”, explained Loon Gangte of DNP+.

The decision follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020—one by Eldred Tellis (Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust) and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and Médécins Sans Frontières Access Campaign, and the other by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from TWN.

The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015. They argued that combining these known medicines did not constitute an inventive step warranting a new patent monopoly.

The Opposition invoked key safeguards under India’s Patents Act, including Section 3(d), which restricts patents on new uses of known substances, Section 3(e), which excludes mere admixtures, and Section 3(i), which excludes methods of medical treatment. The opponents further argued that the application failed to sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. All four grounds were upheld by the Indian Patent Office.

India has the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to WHO estimates, approximately 2.71 million people developed TB in the country in 2024, accounting for a quarter of global cases, with an incidence rate of 187 per 1,00,000 people. Civil society groups are also demanding that the TB Alliance stop the pursuit of proprietary rights over BPaL in other countries.

“Having received public and philanthropic support to develop pretomanid, one of BPaL’s components, they should not be applying for a patent, let alone over frivolous secondary patents on its combination with the other two known medicines,” said Mr. Tellis.

In light of the weak claims by the TB Alliance, Prathibha Sivasubramanian, senior researcher at TWN, endorsed the call for the waiving of patents. “The Indian Patent Office’s decision should serve as a clear signal to the TB Alliance to voluntarily surrender granted patents and to withdraw all corresponding pending applications in other jurisdictions. TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.

articles.title: Can Indian homegrown smartphone brands compete with global giants?
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The government’s goal of establishing a homegrown smartphone brand by October 2028 sets a clear benchmark for national ambition. However, achieving market relevance against global leaders requires moving past price competition and contract assembly

India’s IT Minister, Ashwini Vaishnaw , in a recent interaction with NDTV , outlined an ambitious target that by October 23, 2028, India will have its own mobile phone brand, designed and made locally. While the minister’s intent reflects a strong government policy to foster indigenous manufacturing and self-reliance, translating that vision into commercial success presents steep operational and market hurdles.

The competitive landscape is daunting as Chinese Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) control nearly 70% of India’s smartphone market, as per Counterpoint. Apple, on the other side of the globe, dominates premium market phones . The iPhone maker’s dominance has forced Chinese players to re-evaluate their strategies across price bands.

Ai+, a relatively new domestic smartphone maker, shipped over 10 lakh units in the September ending quarter. And newer entrants like Mivi and Boltt are entering the market at time when the collective market share of India-made smartphones is a modest 7%, per Counterpoint analysis.
But can these brands compete against Apple, Nothing, Samsung, Oppo and Vivo?

Evaluating the 2028 timeline requires a close examination of how Indian smartphone brands have historically performed. For years, domestic players have played catch up with global handset brands instead of driving true innovation — a strategy that has left local firms vulnerable to rapid market shifts.
Domestic manufacturers must need a fundamental shift in their strategy, Faisal Kawoosa, founder of Techarc, said.
“We will have to change our approach to achieving this,” he noted, highlighting two major flaws in the traditional catch-up model.

“First, we have to be subservient to the global supply chain, and our mission’s success depends on how well it serves their business goals,” he explained. “The second challenge is that, since we decide to do our version of something that already exists, by the time we get there, market conditions may have changed, and whatever we achieve might lose relevance. For example, if we focus on, say, the sub-$200 market, customer preferences might shift strongly toward upper tiers, as is happening now.”

Achieving true brand independence demands comprehensive R&D across hardware, software, materials, and apps. Mr. Kawoosa said this foundation cannot be built hastily. “We have to do intensive, broad R&D that also covers materials, electronics, software, hardware, apps, etc. We can’t achieve this in 2 years; it will take at least 5-10 years, provided we do it sincerely,” he stated.
He added that India’s product design capabilities are not yet ready to propose disruptive solutions that attract global supply chains, questioning long-term sustainability by 2028.

articles.title: Wearables data show exercise may help buffer genetic risk for depression
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The researchers analysed survey responses, electronic health records, genetic data and long-term physical activity data from Fitbit devices

An analysis of data from wearables, such as daily steps and minutes of physical activity, showed a consistent pattern where one's genetic risk was less strongly linked to depression severity among more active adults.

"Depression is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, so understanding how we might reduce its burden is important," author Denver Brown, assistant professor in the school of health sciences at Kansas State University, US, said.

"As we move toward more personalised medicine, understanding a patient's genetic risk could help inform conversations about lifestyle, including the potential role of physical activity in helping prevent depression or manage its symptoms," Brown said.

Adding physical activity to a daily routine could therefore be especially beneficial for individuals with a genetic predisposition to depression, potentially helping reduce their risk and ease their symptom burden, the researchers said.

The study, published in the journal Nature Mental Health , analysed data from 23,517 participants of the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide effort in the U.S. to better understand how differences in biology, lifestyle and environment influence health.

"... these findings suggest that genetic and behavioural factors contribute largely independently to MDD (major depressive disorder) onset but interact in shaping symptom expression, highlighting PA (physical activity) as a potential modifier of genetic vulnerability in depression and a potential target for precision mental health interventions," the authors wrote.
The researchers analysed survey responses, electronic health records, genetic data and long-term physical activity data from Fitbit devices.

At the neurobiological level, physical activity enhances neuroplasticity by supporting synaptic plasticity and hippocampal function -- the systems are often dysregulated in depression and implicated in genetic vulnerability pathways, they said.
Exercise also regulates inflammation and improves immune signalling, which the team said is relevant, given growing evidence linking genetic risk for depression to immune and inflammatory signalling.
Further, the researchers said being physically active influences stress reactivity, potentially reducing the impact of genetically mediated stress sensitivity on depressive symptoms.

articles.title: Climate change must be declared 'global health emergency': Lancet study
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Roughly 323,000 deaths have been avoided in "at least" 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016, according to the report
Climate change must be declared a "global health emergency" to shape governments' policies after heat caused three million deaths between 2016 and 2023, a report in The Lancet said Wednesday.

Published by the British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.

Marina Romanello, the executive director of the health and climate research project Lancet Countdown, said there were "three million heat-related deaths globally in an eight-year span since the Paris Agreement" of 2015.
"That's roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat," she told a news conference.
And "68% of those deaths are directly attributable to climate change."
The legally binding international climate treaty adopted in the French capital aimed to limit global warming to well below 2C and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5C compared to pre-industrial levels.
Romanello said the global health emergency due to climate change should have "an integrated approach so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency".
Instead she called for "a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities, and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies moving forward".

To determine the share of deaths attributable to warming caused by human activity, the researchers compiled the number of heat-related deaths recorded by states, then subtracted those that would have occurred in the absence of climate change, said Professor Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney.

articles.title: South Korea fines Google and Apple over ‘unfair’ app market practices
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures

South Korea on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) fined Alphabet's Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country's media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems.

The Commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures.
Google and Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the Commission said.

The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023.

South Korea has for years closely scrutinised the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.

South Korea on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) fined Alphabet's Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country's media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems.

The Commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures.

Google and Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the Commission said.

The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023.

South Korea has for years closely scrutinised the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.
